title: Botnik - Live Procedurally Generated Comedy
speaker: Botnik (Jamie Brew, Steven Barlow, Mike Fredrickson)
summary: The comedy collective Botnik performs pieces written with their predictive text keyboard, which suggests next words drawn from a chosen source corpus rather than common texting language. After a short explanation of the tool and their writing process (a community of about 300 writers in jams, voting on lines that an editor assembles), the bulk of the session is a live performance: a countdown of invented roguelike titles with tips, table reads of generated X-Files and Seinfeld scripts, a Thanksgiving history, a Harry Potter chapter, a Dear Abby video, a cooking video and a Morrissey/P90X song. Design content is limited to the opening description of their human-in-the-loop generation method and how source texts are split per character.

insights.claim: Botnik's predictive writer offers next-word suggestions drawn from a specific source text, such as TED talks, rather than from common texting language, so the output takes on that source's voice.
insights.detail: Botnik contrasts their tool with a phone's predictive text, which predicts from common texts and emails. Fed TED talks about the future, choosing suggestions word by word yields lines in TED's style.
insights.quote: it offers you words that are specific to whatever source text you feed into it

insights.claim: Botnik treats text generation as an instrument where a human author intervenes after every single word, rather than letting a neural net produce a page of output to laugh at.
insights.detail: They say they are less interested in an algorithm that spits out amusing text than in a writer working with the algorithm word by word.
insights.quote: we're really interested in the setting this thing up to be a little bit more like an instrument where an author

insights.claim: Botnik produces pieces through community writing jams where around 300 writers generate lines with a shared keyboard, vote on them, and an editor arranges the best into a script or video.
insights.detail: The community works in a Slack channel with a couple of jams a week; the editor pulls from voted lines to assemble a piece. The roguelike titles and tips in the show were made this way.
insights.quote: write lines and vote on them and an editor will kind of pull from those and arrange them into some kind of a piece

insights.claim: To generate a script, Botnik split X-Files transcripts into separate corpora for Mulder lines, Scully lines and stage directions, using each as its own generative source.
insights.detail: The resulting four-to-five page script was performed as a table read. They used the same idea for Dear Abby, with one source text for questions and one for answers.
insights.quote: breaking the x-files transcripts down into Mulder lines Scully lines and stage directions and use those as separate generative source materials

insights.claim: Combining two unrelated source corpora in one predictive keyboard, such as Amazon reviews of P90X and Morrissey lyrics, produces comic mashups.
insights.detail: Jamie Brew closes the show with a song generated from the combined sources, framed as what Morrissey would write if he reviewed P90X workout DVDs.
insights.quote: I have combined as a source material Amazon reviews of p90x and the collected lyrics of Morrissey
